entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ahmad Sanjar was the ruler of Khorasan from 1097 until 1118, when he became the Sultan of the Seljuq Empire, which he ruled until his death in 1157. During his reign, he expanded the empire's territories, reformed its administrative structures, and promoted trade and cultural exchange. His successors continued to build on his achievements, establishing the Seljuq Empire as a major power in the Islamic world. The empire's legacy can be seen in the many architectural and cultural achievements that still stand today, a testament to the enduring impact of Ahmad Sanjar's rule.

Ahmad Sanjar's significance extends beyond his territorial and administrative reforms, as he also played a key role in the cultural and intellectual developments of the time. He was a patron of the arts and sciences, and his court attracted scholars and intellectuals from across the Islamic world. The famous Persian poet Rumi, for example, was a prominent figure at Ahmad Sanjar's court, and his works would go on to have a profound impact on Islamic literature and culture.

Despite his many achievements, Ahmad Sanjar's legacy is also marked by controversy and conflict. His reign was marked by a series of wars with neighboring kingdoms, and his successors continued to face challenges from external powers. Nevertheless, Ahmad Sanjar's impact on the Seljuq Empire and the wider Islamic world cannot be overstated.

The Seljuq Empire's territorial extent at its peak was approximately 1.2 million square kilometers, stretching from the Indus River in the east to the Mediterranean in the west. This vast territory encompassed much of modern-day Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and parts of Central Asia. The empire's influence extended far beyond its borders, shaping the course of Islamic history and leaving a lasting legacy in the many cultures and civilizations that it touched.
